picks.file: Civitates orbis terrarum. De praecipuis totius universi urbibus. Liber secundus (page 124).jpg
picks.what: Engraving in Braun and Hogenberg, Civitates Orbis Terrarum, vol. 2
picks.why: colored panorama of the city and kasbah drawn on Charles V’s 1535 campaign; trimmed to the Tunis panel (the plate also shows Mahdia and Peñón de Vélez)

picks.what: Engraving in Henri Abraham Chatelain’s Atlas historique
picks.why: colored view labeled Tunis: walled city on its slope beyond the lake, with a harbor fort; ornamental frame mostly cut

picks.file: Tunis, from the Saneeah Eftoor GAC 17669.jpg
picks.what: Steel engraving after Sir Grenville Temple (Government Art Collection)
picks.who: Charles Bentley and James Sands, after Sir Grenville Temple
picks.why: hand-colored view toward the white city with domes and minarets; margins and caption cut

picks.file: Flickr - …trialsanderrors - View from Paris Hotel, Tunis, Tunisia, ca. 1899.jpg
picks.what: View over the medina from the Hôtel de Paris, photochrom print (Library of Congress)
picks.why: color general view over the roofs of the medina to the Zitouna minaret

picks.what: The Zitouna Mosque minaret above the medina, photograph (ETH Library, Zurich)
picks.why: the city’s best-known landmark with the medina roofs stretching to the lake

gaps: P0: no candidates; P6: no modern photograph among the candidates (every “2007” file is an upload of an 1899 photochrom)
notes: #1: Braun and Hogenberg print Johann Maior’s (Jan Vermeyen’s) panorama made during the 1535 siege; horsemen skirmish in the foreground but the city is intact, so not marked as an event. #4 is an uncolored, larger scan of the same panel. #11: the BnF record dates it 1708, but the plate is marked Tome VI of the Atlas historique, which is usually dated 1719; the view is a stylized copy from older sources, so drop it if a firmer P2 is wanted (#9, Nooms’s 1660s painting, shows only a low coast with forts, probably La Goulette). #12: Commons gives 1840 and the Government Art Collection says Temple’s book appeared in 1843; the plate may first have appeared in Fisher’s Shores and Islands of the Mediterranean (1840). #14 is a Library of Congress photochrom; its Commons copy carries a Flickr CC BY 2.0 license (#28 is a smaller framed copy). P5 alternatives: #22 (1932, roofs of the medina toward Bou Kornine) and #27 (1928, aerial view of the medina).
